subtype: Approach: running in panic through the lanes [Pitfall]
passage: From my uncle's shoe stall I saw a boy of about ten sprinting between the lanes, head twisting left and right. His mother, Dolma, I learned later, was running the opposite way, calling his name. The lanes bend, so each time one of them turned a corner the other had already gone through. Once he nearly hit a pole and I called, "Do you know your father's number?" He opened his mouth and only gasps came out. I can't tell what he was thinking; maybe he was too scared to think at all. In the end my uncle stepped into the middle of the lane and waved them both over. - Himani

qa.q: What happened when the narrator asked the boy for his father's number?
qa.a: He opened his mouth and only gasps came out.

qa.q: What might the boy have been feeling as he ran?
qa.a: Terrified, probably, since he was too scared to think and could not even say a number he knew.

qa.q: What could the boy try instead of running, and why?
qa.a: He could stop, breathe and ask a shopkeeper to call, because staying put lets his parents find him and calm lets him remember the number.

qa.q: How does the search look from Dolma's side?
qa.a: Dolma is frightened and calling his name, and because she also keeps moving, each turn takes her past him.

grounding: A child sprints through lanes in panic while the parents also move, so they keep missing each other.

subtype: Approach: running in panic through the lanes [Pitfall]
passage:
Saturday: At the crowded weekly market, Uday let go of his mother's hand to chase a balloon seller. When he turned, she was gone. He ran. Down one lane, up another, shouting. His mother, meanwhile, was running the other way. They missed each other twice. A shopkeeper finally stopped him and asked for his mother's number. Uday knew it, but his mind was blank. The shopkeeper had it announced, and his mother came.
Sunday: At home his cousin Aadhya made him sit. "When you ran, she ran. Next time, stop." They practised the number until he could say it with his eyes shut.
The next Saturday: Before the market, Uday said the number aloud, then took his mother's hand.

qa.q: What did Uday chase at the market?
Why couldn't Uday say the phone number when the shopkeeper asked?
qa.a: He was too frightened; the panic made his mind go blank even though he knew it.

qa.q: What else could Uday's family do to help him remember in a scare?
qa.a: They could write the number on a card in his pocket, so fear cannot take it away.

qa.q: How does the Saturday look to Uday's mother?
qa.a: His mother is terrified, running through lanes and missing him, and hugely relieved at the announcement.

grounding: It shows a child running in panic through the market, missing his parent as both move, while fear blocks the number he knows.

subtype: Approach: running in panic through the lanes [Pitfall]
passage: Siddharth, you're rolling your eyes at me about holding hands at the mela? Let your Leela Nani tell you about my little brother, Gopu. At the Dussehra fair, when he was your age, he let go of my hand to see the effigy. When he couldn't find us, he ran. He ran one way; we ran the other. Round and round the fair, all of us running, never meeting. A policeman finally caught him by the arm and asked where he lived. Gopu knew our address by heart. He had recited it that very morning. But he just cried and couldn't say it. It was an hour before they announced his name and we came. Your great-grandmother didn't let go of him for a week.

qa.q: How long was it before they announced Gopu's name?
How was Gopu feeling when he couldn't say the address?
qa.a: He was so frightened that he just cried, and the fear blocked what he knew by heart.

qa.q: What choice in the story made things worse, and what could Gopu have done instead?
qa.a: Running was the choice that made things worse; he could have stopped where he was, so the family could find him.

qa.q: How might Gopu's mother have felt during that hour?
qa.a: She must have been terrified and desperate, and so relieved at the end that she wouldn't let him go for a week.

grounding: An elder recalls a young brother who ran in panic at a fair, kept missing his family and could not say the address he knew because of fear.
